sections.heading: How Our Roofing Contractors Perform Roof Thermal Imaging Inspections

runs.v: Scanning Under ASTM C1153 Optimal Conditions

c.v: Newark Quality Roofing schedules a thermal imaging scan for the ASTM C1153 optimal conditions and scans after sunset on a clear day, the window that produces the sharpest wet-insulation contrast.

runs.v: Those conditions are no appreciable rain in roughly the prior 48 hours, a dry surface clear of standing water, snow, and debris, wind under about 15 mph, and a temperature differential of roughly 18°F, per ASTM C1153 via IIBEC and Fluke. Winter narrows the contrast to roughly 5°F against roughly 20°F in summer, and the Newark climate poses challenges for roofing due to seasonal weather extremes.
Infrared Imaging and Core Verification

c.v: Newark Quality Roofing flags every warm anomaly and verifies it before reporting it as wet insulation.

runs.v: Modern thermal imaging cameras detect temperature differences of about 0.2°F, and wet-area anomalies range from roughly 0.5°F to 30°F, per IIBEC and Fluke, which is why specialized, high-resolution cameras are essential for accurate results in roofing.
Wet-Insulation Mapping and Condition Reporting

c.v: Newark Quality Roofing maps the verified wet-insulation footprint to the roof plan and reports the moisture extent that sizes a repair or replacement scope.

runs.v: Where a core cut leaves the extent uncertain, nuclear moisture gauges, or electrical impedance scanners under ASTM D7954, can confirm the thermal finding.

sections.heading: What a Thermal Scan Shows: Heat Signatures in the Infrared Spectrum

runs.v: All objects emit infrared energy, the band of the electromagnetic spectrum just beyond visible light that the human eye cannot see, and a specialized thermal imaging camera measures it as surface temperature variations in images of apparent temperature. Different materials retain and release heat at different rates, and thermal imaging is useful for roof inspections because of the water retention characteristics of roofing materials: wet insulation and saturated components give off heat signatures the naked eye would never catch. On a roof after sunset, moisture reads warm; during the day, and on wet ceilings indoors, thermal imaging detects moisture by identifying cool signatures, because wet materials warm slowly and lose heat to evaporation.

Air gaps create distinct thermal anomalies too, so the same scan shows insulation gaps and insulation deficiencies, and thermal imaging identifies energy efficiency issues in roofs and across the building envelope, the building science side of the survey. Thermal imaging also facilitates aerial assessments of large roofing surfaces by drone or aircraft.

Thermal Imaging vs. a Physical Inspection

A thermal scan reads the roof surface; a physical inspection checks flashing, seams, drains, and the attic by hand, and safety and roof access limit what either one can inspect. The images are only as good as the interpretation: certified thermographers need proper training in thermodynamics and environmental conditions, so ask any inspector or roofing contractors who will read the images and what knowledge and training they bring.

faqs.q: What standard governs a roof thermal imaging inspection?

runs.v: ASTM C1153, the Standard Practice for Location of Wet Insulation in Roofing Systems Using Infrared Imaging, governs a roof thermal imaging inspection, per ASTM and the NRCA.

faqs.q: How does thermal imaging find wet insulation in a roof?

runs.v: Thermal imaging inspections typically utilize a temperature differential to identify moisture: wet insulation cools more slowly than dry insulation, so after sunset the wet area stays warmer and reads as a warm anomaly.

faqs.q: Can a thermal imaging inspection be done during the day?

runs.v: A roof scan runs after sunset following a clear sunny day, when the wet area holds a sharp warm contrast; daytime scans are less reliable.

faqs.q: Does thermal imaging find the exact leak entry point?

runs.v: No. Thermal imaging locates wet insulation, and the wet footprint often sits away from the breach; a core cut, probe, or moisture meter verifies each anomaly.

faqs.q: Why does a thermal imaging inspection require a core cut?

runs.v: ASTM C1153 requires every suspected wet area to be verified, because a thermal anomaly alone is not diagnostic: a structural member, rooftop equipment, or an interior heat source can produce one too.

faqs.q: Can thermal imaging replace a physical roof inspection?

runs.v: No. The scan finds concealed wet insulation, while a physical roof inspection finds membrane damage, open seams, and deteriorated flashing, per the NRCA and IIBEC.
